entities.name: Temple of Hera, Olympia
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Hera at Olympia (Heraion of Olympia) in the Peloponnese, built c. 600 BCE — making it one of the oldest surviving monumental Greek temples — was originally a joint temple to both Hera and Zeus before Zeus received his own separate colossal temple (c. 460 BCE). The Heraion is archaeologically revolutionary: it shows the transition from wooden to stone columns in the most direct way possible — some columns were still wooden when the classical traveler Pausanias visited in the 2nd century CE, preserving the history of Greek architectural development within a single building.

Olympia was the site of the ancient Olympic Games (traditionally begun 776 BCE), and the Temple of Hera housed some of antiquity's most precious objects: the famous archaic Hermes of Praxiteles (or its Praxiteles school) was found here, and the chest of Cypselus (an elaborate cedar chest described by Pausanias) was kept in the temple. The Hermes of Praxiteles — if genuine — would be the only original marble statue by a great 4th-century BCE Greek master in existence, making it one of the most debated works in ancient art history.

The Temple of Hera is also the origin point for the modern Olympic torch relay: the Hestia altar within the Heraion precinct is where the Olympic flame is kindled by a high priestess using a parabolic mirror to concentrate sunlight, preserving the ancient sacred fire tradition. This ceremony — revived for the 1936 Berlin Olympics and continued ever since — connects the modern Olympic movement directly to the ancient Heraion of Olympia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Hera at Olympia — Greece's oldest surviving monumental temple, site of the Hermes of Praxiteles, origin point of the modern Olympic torch relay, and a unique record of wooden-to-stone architectural transition — is one of the most historically layered sacred sites in the ancient world.
